newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Pope to pray for peace in first Sarajevo visit.
newsitem.headline: Pope to pray for peace in first Sarajevo visit.

text.p: Pope John Paul II will honour a city which endured 3-1/2 years under brutal siege when he pays a historic visit to the Bosnian capital Sarajevo on Saturday.
Despite declining health and concerns about security, the Pope has decided to travel to the city which was often in his prayers during the violent collapse of old Yugoslavia.
He was scheduled to land late on Saturday afternoon at an airport which only recently opened to commercial flights and still bears the marks of the 1992-95 war.
The Vatican said the 76-year old Pontiff plans to call for religious tolerance and reconciliation during his 25-hour visit at a time of tense relations inside the country's Moslem-Croat Federation.

Although Bosnian political leaders, NATO officers and ambassadors will attend the arrival ceremony, Sarajevo has no mayor to greet the Pope because of political deadlock between Croat and Moslem parties.
The NATO-led peace force and Bosnian authorities enforced elaborate security precautions on Saturday, mindful of a series of bombing attacks on Catholic churches and Islamic mosques since February.

Italian soldiers with sniper rifles patrolled the streets in the city's old quarter as NATO helicopters buzzed overhead. Portugese soldiers parked their armoured vehicles on hills around the stadium where the Pope will hold mass on Sunday.

While NATO spokesmen insisted primary responsibility for security rested with Bosnian authorities, the alliance has reinforced the city with hundreds of troops and helped police draw up security measures.
The Bosnian interior ministry said more than 11,000 police were deployed to secure the city and roads used by pilgrims travelling from the southwest and neighbouring Croatia.
A snow storm on Friday night fuelled concern among church officials that many Catholics might decide not to make the trip from Croatia, which is holding elections over the weekend.
The Pope's decision to visit Sarajevo, instead of the mainly Catholic region of Herzegovina, was viewed as a clear rejection of Croat nationalists who have built up a parallel administration.
Workers this week posted a giant placard of the Pope in the city centre and spruced up streets along his designated route, planting flowers and filling in potholes.

When the Pope drives in his glass-topped Popemobile from the airport to the main catheral in the city centre, he will pass through "Sniper's Alley" -- the notorious boulevard where civilians were cut down by gunmen during the war.
At the Cathedral of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in the city centre, the Pope will celebrate vespers with priests, nuns, and seminarians.
The Vatican said he would present to Bosnian Cardinal Vinko Puljic a votive light that has burned for Sarajevo in Saint Peter's Basicilca since January 1994.
The Pope had to cancel a scheduled visit in September 1994 when Serb forces laying siege to the city refused to offer security guarantees.
Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the peacetime collective presidency, agreed to this visit but has refused to attend ceremonies at the airport, citing concerns for his safety.
The Pope is due to meet Krajisnik and Moslem and Croat presidency members on Sunday morning.
